analysis.title: Anatomy Of A $49 Billion Gigawatt: What's Inside An AI Data Center, Who Builds It, And Why The Price Keeps Going Up
key_insights: BofA puts the all-in cost of an average US data center at $49 billion per GW ($49 million per MW), up $20 billion from three years ago. An AI-focused facility costs about $57 billion per GW. Higher IT equipment costs drive $7mn of the $8mn per-MW increase, partly offset by roughly 35% less floor space needed for denser racks.

About 78% of the BofA cost is IT equipment (servers, networking, storage). Servers are $31.4 million per MW, or 64% of the total. Electrical gear is 5%, cooling 3%, and building plus engineering, installation and contractor profit about 11%.

Morgan Stanley, using a Stanford/Cushman & Wakefield breakdown, puts a 1GW gas-powered US AI campus at $60 billion all-in: $41 billion IT hardware (of which $30 billion GPUs) and $19 billion infrastructure. Power is about 5% of cost but is described as the bottleneck for getting projects running.
Servers are a $415 billion market. ODM direct (Taiwanese contract manufacturers) takes 52% and Dell, the largest OEM, has 7%.

In the $30 billion electrical market BofA estimates Schneider at 24%, Eaton 17% and Vertiv 12%, with the six largest vendors near 80%. In the $18 billion thermal market Vertiv leads with 17%, then Johnson Controls at 15%, and others hold 37%. Caterpillar holds 42% of a $12-16 billion generator market. Construction is a $60-80 billion market with about 4% operating margins.
Liquid cooling was $4-5 billion in 2025 and BofA says it is likely to more than double in 2026. BofA counts 30 vendors offering over 100 coolant distribution units.

Morgan Stanley's AlphaWise survey of operators finds Schneider used by 51%, Siemens 37% and ABB 32% in electrical systems. Beijing Sifang Automation is expected to gain share in the UK and US over two years.

BofA lists over $40 billion of data center infrastructure acquisitions since 2024, including Eaton's $9.5 billion purchase of Boyd Thermal, Ecolab's $4.75 billion deal for CoolIT and Flex's $4.4 billion purchase of EPC Power. Nvidia redesigns its rack every two chip generations on a one-year rhythm, which favors suppliers that deliver power and cooling as an integrated system.

Nvidia's Rubin Ultra Kyber rack is expected to draw over 1,000 kW per rack, pushing a move from 480V AC to 800V DC. BofA expects the first power sidecars to ship in 2027, followed later by solid-state transformers. Electrical content per MW moves from $2.54 million to $2.66-2.82 million, but BofA calls this likely conservative because an 800V silicon carbide hot-swap controller costs over $20 versus $2-3 for AC, and solid-state circuit breakers are directionally 5-10x.

Direct-to-chip liquid cooling went from 5-10% of energized IT load in 2024 to 15-20% in 2025 and could exceed 30% in 2026. BofA says investors often overinterpret the comment that Vera Rubin will not need water chillers, since networking, power electronics and storage still need air cooling. Each 1 MW needs about 285 tons of cooling.

BofA estimates global data center spending rose from about $278 billion in 2022 to nearly $1 trillion in 2026 and forecasts $2.1 trillion in 2028 and $2.9 trillion in 2030, a 37% annual growth rate. The 2028 forecast is 122% above what BofA published a year ago. US cloud capex is forecast to top $1.2 trillion in 2028.
BofA expects neoclouds to own 6% of energized global capacity in 2026, up from under 0.3% in 2023. Colocation landlords remain the largest category.

Morgan Stanley sees global installed IT capacity of about 136 GW at end-2026, growing 23% a year to 316 GW by 2030 (+180 GW, of which US +88 GW, China +49 GW, Europe +12 GW). The bull case is 377 GW and the bear case is 240 GW.
Morgan Stanley's capacity model has Alphabet going from 6.9 GW of owned IT capacity this year to 33.9 GW by 2030, and SpaceX terrestrial data centers growing 72% a year.

Bernstein finds a 59-186 GW spread across 63 forecasts from 40 sources for US 2030 capacity, and end-2025 estimates range from 30 to 80 GW. Bernstein lands on 149 IT-GW in the US by 2030, adding 19 IT-GW in 2027 and 25 IT-GW in 2028. Morgan Stanley reaches 152 GW from a higher 49 GW starting point versus Bernstein's 34 GW. Only about 35% of the announced pipeline is credible.

Morgan Stanley says build cost rose from $30bn/GW in 2022/23 and is projected at $50-60bn/GW by decade end. Operators report costs up 12% over the past year and expect +15% a year for the next two years (US +17%, China +18%). Builders and suppliers report +11% last year and +15% ahead. Only 1% expect costs to fall.

Inflation drivers per Morgan Stanley: powered land up more than 40% in the US and more than 70% in Europe over five years, US transformers up 40-75% over six years, switchgear above 12% a year since 2021, cooling equipment up more than 30% over five years, gas plants at $3 billion per GW, technical wages up 30%, and a roughly 10% capex premium for liquid cooling. Memory prices rose more than six-fold in a year, and TrendForce sees the memory market rising from about $220 billion in 2025 to about $890 billion in 2026.

At 8% annual build inflation through 2030, total cost rises 50% in five years, taking $49 billion per GW to about $60 billion. At +15% for two years the figure is closer to $76 billion. The author notes these are illustrative paths and not forecasts.

Morgan Stanley expects about 180 GW of new global capacity from 2026 to 2030. At $49-60 billion per GW that is $9-11 trillion, in line with BofA's $10.1 trillion cumulative 2026-2030 spending forecast. At $76 billion per GW it is $13.7 trillion.

Morgan Stanley estimates passive infrastructure at about $16 million per MW in the US and Japan, about $3 million in China and about $7 million in India. Industrial power costs about $145/MWh in Europe and Japan, about $90 in the US and about $60 in Saudi Arabia.
Morgan Stanley projects a 70 GW US power shortfall through 2028 before time-to-power fixes, shrinking to 43 GW after them and 38 GW with Asia spillover. The global shortfall is 49 GW by 2028.

BofA tracks 158 GW of planned on-site gas generation, of which only 2 GW is operating and 24 GW under construction. Power projects that went live in 2025 waited a median of 5.1 years for grid connection. Goldman sees behind-the-meter power supplying 25% of data centers by 2030.

Morgan Stanley counts $471 billion of AI-related debt issuance this year through Oct 20, 2.2x the $216 billion issued in all of 2025. Its AI CDS basket trades more than 60bp wider than CDX IG. AA-rated hyperscalers can keep borrowing while lower-rated hyperscalers and neoclouds may need more secured, asset-level financing.

Owners of energized capacity benefit most. Bernstein says new supply is often absorbed shortly after delivery. Morgan Stanley's survey shows US contract pricing for capacity signed in the last three months about 12% higher than a year ago, and Morgan Stanley named Equinix (EQIX) its Top Pick.
The author (ZeroHedge, not a bank desk) thinks the 240 GW bear case is more likely than the 377 GW bull case and expects delays to become common.

market_movers.rationale: Morgan Stanley named Equinix its Top Pick because supply constraints should further strengthen pricing power for incumbents.

sector_views.rationale: Bernstein and Morgan Stanley say owners of energized capacity are best positioned. New supply is absorbed quickly and US contract pricing is about 12% higher than a year ago.

sector_views.sector: Data center electrical and cooling suppliers
sector_views.rationale: Vendors such as Schneider, Eaton, Vertiv, Caterpillar and Johnson Controls are described as charging what the market will bear amid cost inflation, sold-out transformers and consolidation.

sector_views.sector: Data center builders and lower-rated developers
sector_views.rationale: Builders face 2028 prices and financing costs, construction margins are about 4%, and lower-rated hyperscalers and neoclouds may need secured financing.

macro_indicators.indicator: Data center build cost per GW (BofA, US average)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Up $20 billion in three years and the base for cost scenarios of about $60 billion (8% inflation) to about $76 billion (+15% for two years) per GW by 2030.
A 37% annual growth rate. The 2028 figure is 122% above BofA's forecast a year earlier.
2.2x the $216 billion issued in all of 2025, showing financing needs rising with construction costs.

macro_indicators.indicator: Operator-expected data center cost growth (Morgan Stanley AlphaWise)
macro_indicators.reading: +15% a year over the next two years
macro_indicators.interpretation: The US (+17%) and China (+18%) are the highest. Only 1% of respondents expect costs to fall.

crypto_views: Bitcoin miners' powered shells are listed by Morgan Stanley among the time-to-power fixes that cut the US shortfall from 70 GW to 43 GW.

trade_ideas.description: Long Equinix (EQIX), named Top Pick by Morgan Stanley
trade_ideas.rationale: Supply constraints should further strengthen pricing power for incumbents.

risk_factors: Build inflation compounding at double digits (operators expect +15% a year for two years) could push cost per GW to about $76 billion by 2030.
A 70 GW US power shortfall through 2028 and a median 5.1-year grid connection wait for projects that went live in 2025.
Memory prices up more than six-fold in a year and sold-out transformers raise equipment costs.
Credit markets are becoming more selective, and lower-rated hyperscalers and neoclouds may need secured financing.
Only about 35% of the announced US pipeline is credible, so capacity forecasts may be overstated.
Every 10% of inflation on a $10 trillion buildout adds about $1 trillion to be borrowed.
IT hardware is 64-78% of cost and will need replacing in a few years, which ties to server useful-life assumptions.
charts_described: BofA's line-item breakdown puts servers at $31.4 million per MW, or 64% of the $49 million per MW total.

The Stanford/Cushman & Wakefield breakdown used by Morgan Stanley for a 1GW gas-powered US AI campus shows $60 billion total, with $41 billion IT hardware ($30 billion GPUs) and $19 billion infrastructure.

The author's scenario table runs BofA's $49 billion per GW under three inflation scenarios, reaching about $60 billion by 2030 in the gentle case and about $76 billion if operators' +15% for two years holds.
vol_and_positioning: Morgan Stanley's AI CDS basket trades more than 60bp wider than CDX IG.
geopolitical: China is expected to gain share in electrical equipment through Beijing Sifang Automation in the UK and US over the next two years, per the Morgan Stanley survey.
Europe adds only 12 GW of capacity by 2030 under Morgan Stanley's model, which the author attributes to regulation.
cross_bank_references: Morgan Stanley reaches 152 GW of US capacity by 2030 from a 49 GW starting point, almost the same as Bernstein's 149 IT-GW from 34 GW.
Morgan Stanley's cost and capacity figures are set against BofA's $10.1 trillion cumulative 2026-2030 spending forecast.
Goldman sees behind-the-meter power supplying 25% of all data centers by 2030 (Sep 27).

tension_points.bull_case: Morgan Stanley forecasts 316 GW globally by 2030 (bull case 377 GW). BofA says much of the spending is already financed, permitted and contracted, and Bernstein says new supply is absorbed shortly after delivery.
tension_points.bear_case: Morgan Stanley's bear case is 240 GW. Costs are rising 12-15% a year, only about 35% of the announced US pipeline is credible, and credit markets are becoming more selective. The author considers the bear case more likely.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Build cost inflation slowing to the 5% a year path by 2030 that the 8% average scenario assumes would ease the pressure. The report does not give a specific level that invalidates the bear view.

tension_points.bull_case: Price per unit of compute can fall even as price per rack rises, and BofA's $49 million per MW excludes land and grid hookups.
tension_points.bear_case: Operators expect +15% a year for two years, which takes cost to about $76 billion per GW by 2030 and adds $3-4 trillion to the 2026-2030 bill versus the $10.1 trillion forecast.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Operators' expected +15% a year for the next two years failing to materialize.

theme_stances.key_argument: Compounding build inflation could push cost per GW from $49 billion to $60-76 billion by 2030.
theme_stances.evidence: Price is "almost certainly going to become a sharply-increased focal point

theme_stances.key_argument: Owners of powered capacity gain pricing power because new supply is absorbed shortly after delivery.
theme_stances.evidence: ownership of, or exposure to, energized capacity remains particularly valuable

theme_stances.key_argument: Rising costs, memory inflation and selective credit make the 240 GW bear case more likely than the 377 GW bull case.
